newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 27.

text.p: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- PRU END FIVE YEARS OF BONUS CUTS

The Prudential Corporation has announced that it is to end five years of cutting policyholder bonus rates as it unveiled a 14 per cent increase in operating profits, to 691 million stg. Chief executive, Peter Davis, said the company was helped by being able to put a high proportion of its investments into high- yielding equities and property. Prudential is one of the declared bidders for mutual life assurer Scottish Amicable, however Davis said he would not overpay for the company, and if the bid losses he will look to another assurer.
-- PACE FOUNDER GOES AS PROFITS FORECAST FALLS

Pace Micro Technology, the television decoder maker, has shocked the market with its second profits warning in under a month and the departure of Barry Rubery, co-founder and joint chief executive. Peter Morgan, chairman, said Rubery had to go because of differences in management style and he blamed Rubery for a "lack of consultation" which made it difficult for the
board to exercise its duties.
-- SIEBE'S OFFER FOR WHESSOE COUNTERED BY 53 MILLION STG BID

Navia of Norway and Endress and Hauser of Switzerland has trumped Siebe's 46 million stg agreed offer for Whessoe with a 53 million stg bid. The group's directors said they will meet as soon as practicable to consider the cash offer. Siebe said it would respond at an appropriate time. Analysts believe it is possible Siebe will put forward a higher offer.
THE TIMES
-- BAE CONFIDENT OF SINGLE CURRENCY MEMBERSHIP

Leading British exporter British Aerospace has said that the next government will join a European single currency, irrespective of who wins the general election. Chief executive Richard Evans said the main political parties are committed to securing British membership of monetary union and are striking Euro-sceptical notes to appease fringe supporters. BAe and other exporters have been lobbying for British membership that would iron out exchange rate fluctuations and help to reduce the financial risks of selling products to foreign clients.
-- STRONG POUND STILL HAS TO HIT EXPORTS

Figures are released which suggest that the rise in sterling has not yet hurt exporters after the trade deficit narrowed unexpectedly in December. The global trade deficit declined from 1.04 billion stg in November to 854 million stg in December, against market expectations of a 1.1 billion stg gap. The deficit with non-EU countries also showed an improvement in January. The full-year figures show a widening of the deficit,
driven by strong oil exports.
-- BARCLAYS BUYBACK SUFFERS SETBACK

Barclays Bank has run into difficulty over its bid to return excess capital to its shareholders through a buyback scheme. Barclays had set aside up to 300 million stg for the present buyback with a possible 200 million stg more to come during the year, however the bank mopped up on nine million shares for 100 million stg. The lack of success could have been because the institutions wanted to get as high a price as possible for selling their shares while the bank wanted to be seen as being prudent with shareholders money, or that special tax breaks for buybacks are no longer available.
THE GUARDIAN
-- FED CHIEF SHAKES WALL STREET

Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan has warned that there should be caution within the US stock market after the recent rise in the Dow Jones to new record heights. The markets took fright at the prospect of an imminent rise in inflation rates to slow down growth and dampen any inflationary threat. Greenspan told the US Congress that economic prospects were quite favourable, however he would not hesitate to raise rates against inflation.
-- LABOUR PROPOSES FAT-CAT PENALTY

Shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown is planning a penalty against fat-cat utility executives who have used pay, pension and share- option deals to reap millions from privatisation. He is to pledge that, under a Labour government, the gas, electric, water and telecoms regulators would be given powers to order price cuts if boardroom pay and perks get out of hand. The scheme is aimed at discouraging boards from agreeing over-generous remunerations deals with senior managers and directors.
-- PRIVATISED RAIL COMPANY TO CUT 1,000 JOBS

Newly privatised Regional Railways North East is to cut more than 1,000 jobs. This is evidence that the new rail passenger companies are to reduce staff by up to 40 per cent in the next two years. The cuts will seriously affect employment in York where RRNE is based. The cuts were expected by senior people in the industry who acknowledge that jobs will disappear as the newly privatised companies try to keep within tight guidelines and produce a profit.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- ALLIED PUBS PULL PLUG ON SKY-HIGH TV COSTS

Allied Domecq is to remove Sky Television from 200 of its branded pubs because of high charges. This is the latest in a line of similar withdrawals by big brewers, including Bass, Greene King and Scottish and Newcastle, who are one of BSkyB's largest sources of viewers for its sports channels. Marketing director, Martin Grialey, said the cost to landlords had increased in recent years to the extent that it was non longer viable in many of its pubs.
-- MCDONALD'S LAUNCHES US FAST-FOOD PRICE WAR

McDonald's Corporation is preparing to unleash a fast-food price war in the US due to competition from Burger King, owned by Grand Metropolitan. The company will also propose giving a free meal to any customer who does not receive their order within 55 seconds of placing it. The sales effort is to be called "Campaign 55" and could trigger price-cutting throughout the US fast-food industry. McDonalds is striving to reverse a recent
drop in market share.
-- INFLATION SHOWS SHARP FALL ON NEW MEASURE

The Office of National Statistics has published a new and lower measure of UK inflation, calculated on the same basis across Europe, which has boosted the UK's chances of meeting the Maastricht criterion on inflation. The harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP) rose by 2.2 per cent in the 12 months to January. It has also emerged that the Treasury and the Bank of England have both become concerned that the current UK retail price index (RPI) overstates inflation.
